content.overview: Section 9 states the effect of registration: from the date of incorporation in the certificate, the subscribers and subsequent members become a body corporate by the name in the memorandum, capable of exercising all the functions of an incorporated company with perpetual succession and a common seal (where it has one), and with power to acquire, hold and dispose of property, and to contract, sue and be sued in its name.
content.glance: Registration creates a body corporate from the date of incorporation; perpetual succession; capacity to hold property and to sue and be sued; separate legal personality (Salomon), subject to limited veil-lifting (LIC v Escorts).
content.study:
Section 9 is the statutory statement of separate legal personality. On registration under s. 7, from the date mentioned in the certificate of incorporation, the company is a body corporate. It has perpetual succession, may have a common seal, and has power to acquire, hold and dispose of property, and to contract and to sue and be sued by its corporate name. This is the foundation of the Salomon principle in Indian statute. Lifting or piercing the corporate veil remains a separate doctrine applied in limited circumstances (fraud, agency, statute), as affirmed by the Supreme Court in LIC v Escorts Ltd.

Case-law batch 1 (2026-10-15)
• Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd [1897] AC 22 (HL): company is a legal person distinct from its members.
• LIC v Escorts Ltd (1986) 1 SCC 264: Salomon principle affirmed; veil may be lifted only in exceptional circumstances.
Primary-report line-level verification of full judgment text remains open. Not COMPLETE_LOCKED.

sections.heading: Body Corporate from Date of Incorporation
sections.body: From the date in the certificate, subscribers and members constitute a body corporate by the memorandum name.

sections.heading: Perpetual Succession
sections.body: The company’s existence continues despite changes in membership.

sections.heading: Capacity
sections.body: Power to acquire, hold and dispose of property; power to contract; power to sue and be sued in its name.

sections.heading: Common Seal
sections.body: A company may have a common seal; use is regulated by the Act and articles.

examples.title: Separate personality
examples.body: A registered company owns property in its own name. Creditors of a member cannot seize company property solely because the member is indebted.

examples.title: Perpetual succession
examples.body: All original members transfer their shares. The company continues as the same legal person under s. 9.

hypotheticals.question: Does the company die when all members die?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Perpetual succession under s. 9 means the company continues as a legal person independent of the identity of its members.

hypotheticals.question: Can the company sue in its own name?
hypotheticals.analysis: Yes. Section 9 confers capacity to sue and be sued in the corporate name.

distinctions.title: Separate personality (s. 9) vs lifting the corporate veil
distinctions.left: Default rule: company is distinct from members
distinctions.right: Exceptional doctrine: disregard personality in limited cases (fraud, statute, agency)

misconceptions.trap: Members and the company are the same legal person.
misconceptions.correction: Section 9 creates a distinct body corporate from the date of incorporation.

misconceptions.trap: The corporate veil can never be lifted.
misconceptions.correction: Personality is the default; veil-lifting remains available in recognised exceptional cases (LIC v Escorts).

cases.name: Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd
cases.point: A company duly incorporated is a legal person distinct from its members. Registration creates a body corporate; the company is not the agent or trustee of the members merely because control is concentrated in one person.
cases.note: Foundational House of Lords authority on separate legal personality; received and applied throughout Indian company law. Not a decision under the Companies Act, 2013.

cases.name: Life Insurance Corporation of India v Escorts Ltd
cases.point: The Supreme Court affirmed the Salomon principle that a company is a legal person distinct from its members. The corporate veil may be lifted only in exceptional circumstances, including where the corporate form is used to perpetrate fraud or improper conduct, where a statute so requires, or in other recognised limited situations.
cases.note: Five-judge bench. Leading Indian authority on separate personality and limited grounds for lifting the corporate veil. Primary-report line-level verification of the full judgment text remains open for COMPLETE_LOCK.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a Section 9 problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. State the effect of registration. II. List perpetual succession and capacities. III. Note the date of incorporation. IV. Distinguish veil-lifting if raised (Salomon / LIC v Escorts). V. Conclude.

examTips: State personality from the certificate date.
Cite Salomon and LIC v Escorts for personality and veil.
Mention veil-lifting only as an exception.
revisionPoints: Capacity to hold property and to sue
